subject: Climate & Environment
title: Supply Chain Transparency
description: A quick, practical guide to Supply Chain Transparency.

hook.text: Your chocolate bar may contain cocoa grown on land that was rainforest five years ago.

buildup.text: Commodities like soy, beef, cocoa, and palm oil drive most tropical deforestation.

discovery.text: The EU now requires importers to prove their products are deforestation-free.

twist.text: Tracing a supply chain from supermarket shelf to forest plot is technically possible but rare.

climax.text: Blockchain and DNA testing can verify where products came from — down to the exact farm.

punchline.text: Knowing where your food grew is the first step to saving forests.

quiz.question: What does the EU now require from commodity importers?
options: A carbon tax on all imports

details.summary: Supply chain transparency requires companies to trace commodities like soy, beef, palm oil, and timber back to their origin to verify they are not linked to deforestation. The EU Deforestation Regulation now mandates that imports be deforestation-free with proof.
details.whyItMatters: Consumer countries drive deforestation through commodity imports. Mandatory supply chain due diligence shifts the burden from producer countries to the companies and markets that profit.
takeaways: The EU Deforestation Regulation took effect for major traders in 2024
It covers soy, beef, palm oil, wood, cocoa, coffee, and rubber
Satellite verification and geolocation data enable origin tracking

faq.question: How does the EU Deforestation Regulation work?
faq.answer: Companies must prove with geolocation data that commodities were produced on land not deforested after December 2020. Non-compliance results in fines proportional to the environmental damage. It covers seven key commodities and their derivatives.

faq.question: Can supply chain traceability stop deforestation?
faq.answer: It is a powerful tool but not sufficient alone. Laundering through intermediaries, shifting exports to less regulated markets, and deforestation for domestic use can circumvent supply chain rules. Comprehensive policy needs both demand and supply-side measures.
